Aerial Wildlife Survey Report
Wildlife Management Unit 357 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2024)
Classification: Public
Background
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 357 is located in 
West-central Alberta, covering an area of 6939 km 2. 
Surrounding the City of Grande Prairie, WMU357 is bordered 
by British Columbia to the west, the Smoky River to the 
east, and the Green Zones in the north (Saddle Hills) and 
south. The WMU was last surveyed in 2015, with population 
estimates for moose, elk, mule deer and white-tailed deer. 
The objective of this survey (2024) was to update the 
population estimate, and population ratio for sex and age 
classes for moose, mule deer, white-tailed deer and a total 
minimum count for elk in WMU 357.
Survey Method
The aerial survey for moose, deer, and elk in WMU 357 was 
conducted between February 27 th and March 2nd, 2024. 
Distance sampling transect methods (AEP 2016, Buckland et 
al., 2001) were used to estimate the abundance and density of 
moose and deer in WMU357. Transects (N = 709) up to 10 km 
in length, and oriented north-south, (Fig. 1) were established 
throughout the unit with 1.2 km spacing. A random sample 
(n = 230) of these transects was flown during this survey. The 
unit was stratified into 2 strata areas: High Density and Low 
Density based on mule deer and white-tail deer densities 
from previous surveys. This stratified approach to sampling 
was used to increase the precision of deer estimates and 
increase survey efficiency. Moose and deer were classified by 
age (adult or young) and sex. Antler classes were assigned 
to both species (ASRD 2010) of deer and moose (small, 
medium, large), and elk (maximum point estimates). Moose 
with hair loss, associated with the progression of winter tick 
were classified into categories of hair loss associated with the 
severity of tick infestations (AEP 2016)..
While transect sampling methods provide reliable estimates 
for moose and deer, they are not effective for estimating elk 
densities because elk are highly clumped in large groups and 
estimates using transect sampling are generally imprecise. 
Therefore, while all elk observed during the distance sampling 
transects are classified and counted, an additional dedicated 
survey was conducted (an additional 7 hours) to locate elk 
groups that were not observed on transects. This additional 
effort focused on areas where elk are known to occur, 
have been observed (e.g. tracks or crop damage) or areas 
with high quality habitat that were not surveyed during the 
transects.
Results
A total survey effort of 1691.5 km, and 60.7 hours of flight 
time. Survey conditions were considered good, with a fresh 
snow fall with full coverage in all habitat types contributed to 
optimal detection of animals and facilitated tracking of groups 
(for elk minimum total count).
In total, 513 moose were observed on transects from 341 
independent group observations. A total of 460 moose were 
classified of which 247 were cows, 118 were calves, and 95 
were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 95% had already shed 
their antlers at the time of the survey. Of those that still had 
antlers (n=5), all were considered small (small spike or forked 
antlers). The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.39 (95% 
CI 0.30–0.48) and 0.41 (95% CI 0.34 – 0.48), respectively. 
Twenty percent of the moose observed had slight tick rub 
(<25% of total body surface), 6% had moderate tick rub 
(≥25% but <50% of total body surface), and 5% had severe 
tick rub (≥50% of total body surface). The density estimate 
was 0.59 moose/km2 with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 
9.5% (90% CI 0.51-0.69). The estimated moose population for 
WMU 357 was 4132 (90% CI 3551–4807). See Table 1 for a 
comparison to previous survey results. The moose population 
is estimated to have increased by 66.9% since the 2014/2015 
survey, representing an annual average (geometric mean) 
population growth rate of 1.06 (90% CI 1.03-1.09.
In total, 882 mule deer were observed on transects from 132 
independent groups. Of the 709 total mule deer that were 
successfully classified, there were 337 does, 218 fawns and 
154 bucks. Of the bucks that could be reliably classified, 7% 
were antlerless, 56% were small (1 or 2 points), 33% were 
medium (3 or four points on at least one antler) and 4% were 
large (at least 4 points, with an antler spread beyond the 
ears). The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.47 (95% CI 
0.26 – 0.67) and 0.65 (95% CI 0.54 – 0.75), respectively. The 
density estimate was 0.57 mule deer/km 2 with a CV of 17.3% 
(90% CI 0.43 – 0.75). The estimated mule deer population 
for WMU 357 is 3933 (90% CI 2963–5221). See Table 2 for 
a comparison to previous survey results. The mule deer 
population is estimated to has increased by 59% since the 
2014/15 survey, representing an annual average (geometric 
mean) population growth rate of 1.05 (90% CI 0.99-1.10).
We observed 1313 white-tailed deer on transects from 263 
groups. Of the 867 that were successfully classified, there 
were 433 does, 345 fawns, and 89 bucks. Of the bucks

that could be reliably classified, none were antlerless, 46% 
were small (1 or 2 points), 48% were medium (3 or 4 points 
on at least one antler) and 6% were large (at least 4 points). 
The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.21 (95% CI 
0.14–0.28) and 0.79 (95% CI 0.66 – 0.93) respectively. The 
density estimate was 1.3 white-tailed deer/km 2 with a CV of 
11.0% (90% CI 1.09-1.56). The estimated white-tailed deer 
population for WMU 357 is 9054 (90% CI 7563-10839). See 
Table 3 for a comparison to previous surveys. The white-tailed 
deer population has grown by 130% 2014/15 survey, 
representing an annual average (geometric mean) population 
growth rate of 1.09 (90% CI 1.05-1.14).
A total count of 2456 elk in 125 groups were observed 
from transects and additional search effort in areas outside 
transects. Of the 1882 elk that were successfully classified, 
1135 were cows, 446 were calves, and 241 were bulls. Of 
the bulls that could be reliably classified, 10% had no antlers, 
63% were small (1 or 2 point), 12% were medium (3 to 5 point) 
and 15% were large (six point or greater). At this time of year, 
most bull elk still have antlers so these proportions should be 
representative of the population post-hunting season. The 
bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.21 and 0.39, respectively 
(note: CI’s are not available for total counts). Comparison to 
previous survey results can be found in Table 4.
